scenarios.title: A small team changes its deployment rule

entities.description: release engineer on the Tide project

work_context.purpose: Review the current Tide deployment gate and its history
open_questions: Which observations support the release procedure?

events.text: Lin proposed releasing Tide after one reviewer signs the checklist. Mei agreed to try that rule for the first internal deployment.
One reviewer approved Tide, but a rollback setting escaped review. Lin stopped the deployment; Mei traced the missed setting to the single-person checklist.
Lin and Mei replaced the one-reviewer rule. Tide now uses the private term double-lamp gate: two independent reviewers must sign the same recorded deployment checklist before release.
Mei calls the same two-signature requirement the paired-light check. It is an alias for the double-lamp gate, not an extra approval stage.
On the next Tide release, Lin reused the double-lamp gate. Mei and a second independent reviewer signed the checklist; Lin then deployed.

Lin clarified that approval readiness and service readiness are different. The double-lamp gate concerns reviewer signatures; warm-start readiness concerns a successful health probe. Passing the health probe never substitutes for either signature.
Mei joked that the old checklist looked like a purple turnip. Nobody adopted that phrase as a policy, project name, or reusable procedure.
The Tide audit recorded both signatures before deployment and a separate successful health probe afterward. Mei confirmed that the one-reviewer rule is historical and no longer applies.

concepts.meaning: service readiness established by a health probe

expected_maintenance.merge_expectation: double-lamp gate and paired-light check refer to one concept; if both Tags formed, merge with provenance
expected_maintenance.split_expectation: approval readiness and service readiness must remain distinct; if initially conflated, split in explicit scope

scenarios.title: A preference changes across recurring sessions

work_context.purpose: Review Aya current writing preference with dated evidence

events.text: Aya preferred writing the field journal late at night because the laboratory was quiet. This was her stated preference for the first week.
After two late-night writing sessions Aya found mistakes in the next morning measurements. She attributed the mistakes to fatigue, not to the journal itself.
Aya changed her preference to writing the field journal after breakfast. She explicitly retired the late-night routine; the journal format stayed the same.
Aya wrote after breakfast again and checked the measurements before laboratory work. She said the morning routine was easier to sustain.
Aya repeated the breakfast journal routine in a new session. She still preferred morning writing and did not resume the old night routine.
A visitor suggested an unrelated midnight exercise schedule. Aya did not adopt it and said it was not her journal preference.

expected_maintenance.accretion_expectation: recurring independent dated events reinforce a stable center; meaningful use can improve usefulness without changing the observed epistemic class

scenarios.title: Two same-name people and an analogy between incidents

entities.description: tooling engineer investigating stale build outputs
compiler artifact cache with consumer leases

work_context.purpose: Find source-supported analogies for a stale consumer failure
open_questions: Does an active consumer protect an old asset?

events.text: Storage Sam found that the snapshot service deleted an old snapshot while an active reader still held its lease. The reader failed when opening its second block.
Storage Sam changed snapshot reclamation: retired snapshots remain until their last reader lease is released. This fixed the second-block failure.
The snapshot review recorded the procedure: retire the old snapshot, wait for all reader leases to end, then delete it. A running reader must keep one consistent snapshot.

Tools Sam found a compiler consumer reading an old build artifact after cache cleanup deleted that artifact. The symptom resembled the snapshot reader failure, although the systems and engineers were different.
Storage Sam showed Tools Sam the snapshot reader-lease procedure. Tools Sam used the analogy to separate retirement from deletion in the build cache.
Tools Sam implemented consumer leases for build artifacts: retire first, reclaim after the last consumer releases. The stale consumer failure stopped in the next build.
The joint verification found that both fixes preserved active consumers while allowing retired assets to be reclaimed afterward. Snapshot and build cache were not merged into one system.
The daily summary used broad words such as work, problem, and project for many unrelated activities. Those generic words supplied no causal evidence connecting the snapshot and build incidents.

concepts.meaning: protect active consumers; retirement precedes safe reclamation

expected_maintenance.hub_expectation: generic broad concepts must not dominate the specific consumer-lease path
